headline: High: shared filesystem and broad egress make prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible; slim's privileged container actions raise the blast radius.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Khoj reads indexed personal notes/files and has broad network egress; slim reads/writes container artifacts and runs an interactive CLI. No shared channel is explicit, but if Khoj ingests slim-produced files or logs, prompt-like content could be treated as trusted. The pairwise bridge is inferred, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF Khoj indexes or displays slim-generated files/logs as chat context, injection becomes reachable.
IF an operator copies slim output into Khoj without sanitization, malicious instructions can propagate.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of slim logs into Khoj.
Strip instructions from any files passed between agents.
Use a read-only handoff folder with human review.
Add a prompt-injection warning banner to imported artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Khoj touches personal notes and indexed documents, while slim handles filesystem artifacts, environment variables, and certificate private keys. Both have filesystem read access and broad egress, so a shared workspace or copied artifacts could leak sensitive data from either side. The profiles do not prove a shared workspace, so this is inferred rather than direct.
conditions: IF both agents access the same directory, sensitive notes or keys can cross between them.
IF slim is pointed at a workspace containing Khoj notes, those notes may be exposed in outputs or uploads.
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent.
Keep secrets out of any shared directory.
Run slim on sanitized copies only.
Review outbound network destinations for both agents.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Khoj cannot write the filesystem and slim can, so direct write-write conflict is limited. Both can read files and both have broad egress, but the rubric's high/medium conflict indicators require overlapping mutable writes or shared OAuth scopes, which are not present. The main risk is operational overlap, not contention.
conditions: IF an external orchestrator gives both agents write access to the same directory, conflict risk rises.
IF slim is configured to rewrite artifacts that Khoj indexes, stale reads may occur.
mitigations: Keep Khoj read-only.
Point slim at a separate output directory.
Use file locks if a shared directory is unavoidable.
Schedule agents sequentially instead of concurrently.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Khoj produces retrieved answers from personal notes, and slim is an interactive CLI that can execute commands and modify container artifacts. If slim treats Khoj output as authoritative, a mistaken retrieval can cascade into destructive container changes. No verification step is documented in the pair, so the pathway is plausible in default operator workflows.
conditions: IF slim consumes Khoj answers as command guidance without verification, errors can propagate.
IF Khoj retrieves stale or irrelevant notes that slim then operationalizes, downstream actions may be wrong.
mitigations: Require human verification before slim acts on Khoj output.
Ask Khoj for sources and cross-check them manually.
Limit slim to dry-run mode for first-pass actions.
Log and review any command derived from retrieved text.

E_compliance.rationale: Khoj explicitly touches personal notes and indexed documents, while slim handles certificate private keys, environment variables, and registry credentials. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, so only a generic compliance gap exists: sensitive data classes differ and could be retained or logged differently. The other agent is cited because the risk arises from their combined handling of sensitive classes.
conditions: IF either agent logs or retains the other's sensitive data class longer than policy allows, compliance drift occurs.
IF EU personal notes are processed through a non-compliant slim deployment, residency issues may arise.
mitigations: Confirm retention settings for both agents.
Exclude secrets from shared logs.
Document which data classes each agent may process.
Use separate compliance policies for notes and container secrets.
